Christopher Oct 10, 2026 7:38 AM October 10, 2026 7:38 AM Advertisement AP Photo/Fernando Vergara, FILE Who was Irena Sendler? If you don’t know, don’t worry. Most people don’t know who she was. And that’s a problem. I myself didn’t know who she was until very recently, and when I found out why I didn't know, the reasons made me angry. Because my ignorance was a result of what we value as a society. Advertisement Irena Sendler was a Polish nurse who lived in Warsaw during the German occupation. Unlike almost all Muslims, most contemporary Europeans, and half of contemporary Americans, Sendler witnessed the antisemitic genocide occurring all around her and knew that it was wrong. As a nurse whom the Department of Social Welfare and Public Health employed, she had special access to the Jewish ghetto that most people didn’t. She used that access to smuggle food and medicine in, and to smuggle people out. She conspired with the Polish Underground to forge identity documents for Jews , and to help find them hiding places outside of the ghetto. She found homes for Jewish children and orphans with Polish families, Catholic parishes, and nuns' convents. The children were given Christian names and taught Christian prayers, in case the Germans questioned them. Though a practicing Catholic herself, Sendler didn’t want the children’s Jewish identities erased. She kept meticulous records of each child and orphan who was given a new identity and hidden with a new family, to include the children’s original names and family origins. She kept these documents in jars, buried in the ground, so that after the war, there was a possibility of reunification. Whenever she was working in the ghetto, she would wear a yellow Star of David to show solidarity with the people she was trying to help. Giving assistance to Jews in the Warsaw ghetto was a crime punishable by death, not only to the perpetrator but to their entire family. Sendler and her friends risked this on a daily basis. In October 1943, the Gestapo arrested her on suspicion of insurrectionary activity. Despite being brutally and repeatedly beaten and tortured, Sendler betrayed not a single Polish comrade or Jewish refugee. She was scheduled to be executed, but managed to escape after the Polish Underground bribed one of her German guards. Recommended Meet Brandon Johnson, the 'Descendant of the Formerly Enslaved' A.J. Christopher This Liberal Lawyer Says Ilhan Omar Is in Serious Trouble Matt Margolis Advertisement A month later, she was back to helping smuggle Jewish children out of the ghetto. By the end of the war, it is estimated she saved over 2500 Jewish children from extermination. Sendler survived the war, and continued to help children. She dug up the jars with the children’s information and gave it to the Jewish Committee, which did what it could to reunite the shattered families. During her life, she never once asked for recognition or compensation of any kind. People like her never do. Sadly, the world doesn’t know about Irena Sendler. The world almost knew about Irena Sendler. Almost two decades ago, the Israeli and Polish governments nominated Sendler for the Nobel Peace Prize. It would seem like a no-brainer that a young, unarmed nurse who saved thousands of children from Nazi extermination, and who endured torture and imprisonment for her efforts, would be a shoo-in. Instead, the Nobel Committee gave the award to a soapbox preaching nepo baby who made a fifth grade-level PowerPoint presentation about how the world was going to melt if we didn’t purchase the indulgences (i.e. carbon credits ) he was peddling, which made him richer than he already was. He owns a 400-acre farm and a 10000 square foot mansion, along with additional coastal property. His homes consume 20 times more electricity than the average American home. But he thinks you and I consume too much. As a result of green policies he advocated for, tens of millions of people in places such as South Africa and Indonesia were pushed back into absolute poverty. Advertisement None of his apocalyptic prophecies ever came to fruition, and he has never apologized for them. That grinning snake oil salesman accepted his Nobel Prize in December 2007. Irena Sendler died five months later. Nearly twenty years on, nothing has changed. The Nobel Committee just awarded this year’s prize to former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay, an antisemitic, anti-American globalist and terrorist apologist. She has supported butchers such as Zimbabwe’s Robert Mugabe, so long as his victims were the right color, and would have been only too happy to have seen people such as Irena Sendler fail in their efforts. What a sick, sick society we live in. Help continue to tell the truth about the genocidal left as we continue to usher in the Golden Era of America. https://www.politico.eu/article/costa-cu.text: BRUSSELS — António Costa aims to shave another €44 billion off the EU’s planned seven-year budget, according to a fresh set of numbers unveiled on Saturday. For the first time since the budget negotiations began last year, EU regional spending, known as cohesion policy, is a target for reductions. The European Council president proposed reducing it by €8 billion compared with the last proposal, while farmers’ subsidies remained untouched. This is a major setback for a coalition of 17 countries from Eastern and Southern Europe — including Poland, Italy and Spain — who rejected potential cuts to cohesion policy only a few days ago. However, the plan was welcomed as "a first step" by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who urged further cuts. Advertisement Advertisement "This proposal is fit for tackling the challenges we are facing in our societies, and gives the European Union the necessary capacity to act," Costa said on Saturday morning. Costa, who is guiding discussions over the 2028-2034 budget which needs to be agreed by all EU governments, suggested the reductions, which are based on current prices, from the previous proposal presented by Ireland , in its role holding the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, last month. Overall, the cuts amount to a reduction in size of the budget by €204 billion, or 10.2%, from the European Commission’s original proposal in July last year. In another major development, Costa suggested introducing a new tax on large digital companies such as Google and Meta to help finance the budget over the coming years. In recent years, Brussels held back from levying this tax for fear retaliation from Washington, but the Republicans' bruising defeat in the midterm elections earlier this month created an opening. These ideas set the scene for fraught discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during a summit next week. Even then the agreed budget will have to be approved by the European Parliament. Advertisement Advertisement Despite governments disagreeing over the size of the budget, Costa is confident that governments will reach a deal among themselves during a summit of EU leaders starting on Dec. 17. "I believe this proposal can bring us closer to a final agreement. And I will continue to work with all leaders to reach that objective," he said. However, German chancellor Friedrich Merz criticised the cuts as insufficient. “The proposal now on the table is a first step, but its overall size remains too high,” he said in a statement . On the other hand, the European People’s Party’s budget negotiator Siegfried Mureșan immediately criticized Costa’s cuts. The plan “is unacceptable to the European Parliament and cannot form the basis for our consent. The proposed cuts take the negotiations backwards,” he wrote on X . "The proposal now on the table is a first step, but its overall size remains too high," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a statement pointing to tough negotiations ahead. Advertisement Advertisement Big cuts EU governments are split between those that want a smaller budget focused on defense and competitiveness, and those that think it should be larger and spent on traditional priorities such as farming and cohesion. Costa proposed modest cuts to cohesion — which had been spared from previous rounds of cuts due to opposition from many governments — to appease Germany and its allies, the so-called frugals. However, budget savings also came from foreign aid which was cut by €7 billion, and competitiveness which was axed by €20 billion. Another €10 billion savings came from the deferral of the repayments of the EU’s post-Covid debt, which are due to start in 2028. One of the few budget items to receive additional funding was a rainy-day crisis fund that was downsized by Ireland last month. This is seen as a concession to the Commission, which supports more spending flexibility. Advertisement Advertisement Going after big tech Costa proposed new taxes and other adjustments to generate €60 billion annually for the EU budget. Crucially, he replaced an unpopular corporate tax proposal known as CORE, which was put forward by the Commission last year, with a levy on tech multinationals with a turnover exceeding €750 million per year globally and over €50 million in the EU. POLITICO first reported the move earlier this week. The proposed digital levy will cover online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data for companies. It is expected to generate around €5 billion per year, according to an EU official. Most governments opposed CORE — a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — over fears that it would undermine EU competitiveness. To generate additional resources for the budget, Costa also suggested increasing two largely uncontroversial taxes on non-collected plastic and electronic waste that flows directly to the bloc’s budget by levying an additional 25 cents per kilo. Advertisement Advertisement The proposal also envisions a higher share of a carbon imports’ tax that flows to the EU cash pot to 100% from the current 75%, and exploring levies on crypto firms and national spectrum auctions. In a further concession, Costa also suggested phasing in two taxes on tobacco products and polluting firms, known as the Emissions Trading System , for countries that are overwhelmingly affected. Costa argued that the new proposed taxes will keep national contributions to Brussels under control. "With this proposal we have managed to come very close to the current level of national contributions," he said. This article was updated.

https://www.dw.com/en/can-rassvet-russia.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PtKd Prefer DW on Google Electronic warfare is an important component in Russia's war against Ukraine Image: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance Advertisement Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX. Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit. Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine. On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink. Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army. In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated, and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels. In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink. Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's dependence on satellites To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What is Rassvet? Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026. According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks. The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare. HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory." Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027. According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president , the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory. He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there. Starlink terminals are used by both the Russian and Ukrainian armies for communications Image: Lev Radin/picture alliance SpaceX remains far superior to Rassvet in tech terms Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept." "When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase. He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company. He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components." "Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin said. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being." SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors. According to DW sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not currently require as many satellites as Starlink. Ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes. But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos. In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled. Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Did SpaceX throttle Starlink in Ukraine? Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine. "Unfortunately , our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher. Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23. When asked by DW whether the Ukrainian military could gain access to Rassvet, Trishkin said it was "only a matter of time" before terminals fell "into foreign hands and are subsequently examined."
